fr-acqua-pazza: Score each fish with 3–4 deep diagonal cuts on each side, cutting through to the bone — this allows seasoning to penetrate and ensures even cooking. Season inside and out with salt, including into the cavity and the score marks. Allow to rest at room temperature for 10 minutes while you prepare the broth base. Pat the exterior dry with paper towels before adding to the pan.

In a wide, lidded pan large enough to hold the fish flat, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and chili flakes. Cook gently for 1–2 minutes, stirring, until the garlic is softened and just beginning to turn pale gold at the edges — not brown. Add the halved cherry tomatoes, pressing a few gently with the back of a spoon to release their juice. Cook another 2 minutes until the tomatoes begin to soften and the oil takes on their color.

Pour the wine and water into the tomato base and raise heat to bring to a brisk simmer. Lay the seasoned fish flat in the pan — they can overlap slightly if necessary. Spoon some of the broth and tomatoes over the fish. Cover with a lid and cook on medium heat for 12–15 minutes, depending on the size of the fish. The fish is done when the flesh at the deepest score mark pulls away from the bone cleanly and is opaque white all the way through.

Scatter the roughly chopped parsley over the fish and pan. Drizzle a final generous stream of your best extra-virgin olive oil directly over the fish and broth. The raw olive oil added at the end is essential to the dish's character — it emulsifies into the broth as you spoon it over. Serve the fish whole in the pan or carefully transferred to a deep platter with all the broth ladled around it. Provide gluten-free bread to mop the pan.
fr-agedashi-tofu: Remove the tofu from its packaging and wrap in 3-4 layers of paper towels. Place on a flat surface with a small plate on top as a weight — do not use heavy books, which will crush silken tofu. Let rest for 15 minutes to draw surface moisture. Cut into 6-8 cubes, approximately 4x4cm. Very gently pat each cut face dry with paper towels. This step is essential: surface moisture causes the starch coating to dissolve before frying, resulting in a bald, oil-soaked cube rather than a crisp shell.

Combine dashi, usukuchi soy sauce, and mirin in a small saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring to combine. Cook for 2 minutes. Taste — it should be lightly salty, savory with a background sweetness, and clean. The pale soy sauce is traditional for agedashi to preserve the golden color of the sauce; regular soy makes a darker, deeper version. Keep warm until needed.

Heat oil to 180°C (355°F) in a deep, narrow pot or small wok. Working quickly, roll each tofu cube in potato starch, pressing gently to adhere, then shake off excess — you want a thin, even dust, not a thick coat. Lower cubes into oil one at a time using chopsticks or a spider. Fry 3-4 pieces at a time for 2-3 minutes, turning once, until the coating is set and very pale gold. The coating should be almost translucent, not deeply browned.

Place 2-3 fried tofu cubes in a small, deep bowl. Ladle hot tentsuyu sauce over and around them immediately — the sauce should come about halfway up the sides of the cubes. Garnish the top of each cube with a small mound of grated daikon, a pinch of grated ginger, a few strands of katsuobushi (which will wave in the heat), and thinly sliced green onion. Serve within 60 seconds. The entire magic of agedashi is the moment when the crisp coating begins to absorb the broth — this process starts the second you pour the sauce.

fr-akara-bean-fritters: Soak the dried black-eyed peas in cold water for at least 6 hours or overnight. Drain, then rub the beans vigorously between your palms in a bowl of fresh water — the skins will loosen and float to the top. Skim off the skins and drain, repeating 3–4 times until most skins are removed. Clean, skin-free beans produce a white, fluffy akara batter; beans with skins still on make the fritters dense and grey-tinged. Even a 20-minute soak and aggressive rubbing will remove most skins.

Combine the peeled beans, onion, scotch bonnet, salt, and just enough water to help the blender run — start with 2 tablespoons and add more sparingly. Blend until very smooth, about 2–3 minutes. The goal is a thick, smooth, fluffy paste, not a thin pourable liquid. Transfer to a bowl and beat the batter vigorously with a wooden spoon or hand mixer for 3–5 minutes — this incorporates air and gives akara its characteristic lightness. The batter should double slightly in volume and turn paler as air is worked in.

Heat enough oil in a medium saucepan to give a depth of at least 5 cm. Heat to 175 °C (a small drop of batter should sizzle and rise immediately). Using two spoons or a small ice cream scoop, drop spoonfuls of batter gently into the oil — do not crowd the pot, 4–5 at a time. Fry for 3–4 minutes total, turning gently halfway, until deep golden-brown on all sides. The fritters will puff and become round as they fry. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels.

Remove akara with a slotted spoon and drain on a paper towel-lined plate. Serve immediately — hot akara at peak crisp is the entire point of the dish. In Lagos, akara is sold from street stalls in the early morning alongside ogi (fermented corn porridge). Serve with a dipping sauce of tomato, onion, and pepper if desired. Akara made to order, eaten in the street, still crackling from the oil, is one of the great breakfast experiences of West Africa.
fr-al-pastor: Tear the guajillo and ancho chilies open and remove all seeds and veins. Heat a dry comal or cast-iron skillet over medium heat until very hot. Press each chili flat with a spatula and toast for 20–30 seconds per side — until fragrant and pliable, with a couple of small dark spots. Do not let them turn black, or the entire marinade will taste of ash. Transfer immediately to a bowl and cover with just-boiled water. Weight them down with a small plate and soak for 20 minutes until completely soft and yielding.

Drain the chilies, reserving 60ml of soaking water. Combine soaked chilies, achiote paste, pineapple, onion, garlic, vinegar, oregano, cumin, salt, and oil in a blender. Add the reserved soaking water. Blend on high for 2–3 minutes until completely smooth — there should be no visible chili skin or fibre. Taste and adjust: it should be deeply smoky, mildly tangy from the vinegar and pineapple, pleasantly spiced, and the salt should be at the front of your tongue. If too thick to blend, add soaking water one tablespoon at a time.

Place the thinly sliced pork shoulder in a large bowl or zip-lock bag. Pour all of the marinade over the pork and toss thoroughly until every surface is evenly coated in the deep red paste. The pineapple enzymes (bromelain) will begin tenderizing the meat almost immediately — this is why the marinating time should not exceed 8 hours or the pork surface will become mushy. Cover and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours, ideally overnight (but not more than 8 hours for thin-cut shoulder).

Position the oven rack at the highest position and set the broiler to its highest setting. Line a heavy baking sheet with foil. Lay the marinated pork slices in a single layer — they may overlap slightly. Broil for 4–5 minutes until the top surface is caramelised, blistered in places, and the edges are beginning to char. Flip each slice and broil for another 2–3 minutes. Remove and shave or chop into small pieces for tacos. Traditionally, the caramelised, slightly charred bits (the chicharitas off the trompo) are the best part — do not avoid the char.
fr-alfajores: Beat the room-temperature butter and sifted powdered sugar together in a stand mixer with the paddle attachment on medium speed for 4–5 minutes until the mixture is very pale, almost white, and light in texture. The prolonged creaming incorporates air and fully dissolves the powdered sugar, which is essential to the eventual melt-in-the-mouth texture. Scrape the bowl and paddle halfway through. The final mixture should look like whipped cream cheese — not the dense, yellow paste of under-creamed butter.

With the mixer on low, add the eggs one at a time, then the extra yolk, beating well after each addition. The extra yolk enriches the dough and contributes to the sandy, crumbly texture. Add the vanilla extract and lemon zest. Sift together the cornstarch, flour, and baking powder and add in two additions with the mixer on low, mixing only until just combined — as soon as no dry flour is visible, stop. Over-mixing develops gluten and will make the cookies tough rather than tender. The dough will be soft and slightly sticky.

Preheat the oven to 170°C (340°F). On a lightly floured surface, roll the chilled dough to 5mm thickness — not thinner, or the cookies will be too fragile. Cut 4cm rounds with a cookie cutter and arrange on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spaced 2cm apart. Bake for 12–14 minutes. The key indicator is what should NOT happen: the cookies must not take on any color. They should look almost exactly as they did going in — pale and matte, just dried and set. This near-invisible bake is the secret to their dissolving tenderness.

Ensure the cookies are completely cool — even slight warmth will melt the dulce de leche and cause them to slide apart. Match cookies into same-sized pairs. Spoon or pipe a generous amount of dulce de leche (about 1 teaspoon) onto the flat side of one cookie. Press the matching cookie on top, flat-side down, and rotate very gently to spread the dulce de leche to the edge without cracking the fragile cookies. Roll the exposed dulce de leche edge through the coconut, pressing lightly so it adheres all the way around. Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days.

fr-aloo-gobi: Heat the ghee in a wide, heavy skillet or karahi over medium-high heat. Add the cumin seeds — they should sizzle immediately and begin to darken within 30 seconds. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring frequently, for 8–10 minutes until deep golden and soft. Add the minced garlic and grated ginger and stir for another 60 seconds until the raw smell of the garlic has mellowed to sweet-savory. The entire pan should smell of toasted cumin and caramelizing onion — this is the flavor foundation everything else will absorb.

Add the ground turmeric, ground coriander, and Kashmiri chili powder to the golden onion in the pan. Stir constantly over medium heat for 45–60 seconds, cooking the spices directly in the ghee. The mixture will become very fragrant and stiff; if it begins to stick, add a tablespoon of water and stir to release. Season with salt. The spice paste is ready when the raw dusty aroma of the spices has transformed into a roasted, warm, complex fragrance and the fat has separated slightly at the edges of the paste.

Add the potato cubes to the spiced base and toss to coat every surface in the turmeric-orange spice paste. Spread into a single layer and cook over medium-high heat, stirring every 2–3 minutes rather than constantly — this allows the potato to develop golden sear marks rather than just steaming. Cook for 8–10 minutes until the potato cubes are golden on several sides and half-tender when pierced with the tip of a knife. They should still have a little resistance at this stage; they will finish cooking with the cauliflower.

Add the cauliflower florets to the pan and toss to coat in the spiced ghee. Sprinkle the garam masala over everything now — added at this mid-stage, it blooms gently in the residual fat rather than burning in an empty pan. If the pan looks very dry, add a tablespoon of water and cover with a lid for 3–4 minutes to steam-cook the cauliflower through. Then remove the lid and cook uncovered for another 5 minutes, tossing every 2 minutes, until both the potato and cauliflower are fully tender and the pan is dry — this is a dry curry; no sauce, only fragrant, spiced fat.

Remove the pan from the heat. Squeeze the lemon juice over the entire pan and toss immediately — the acid brightens all the spices and cuts through the richness of the ghee. Scatter the fresh cilantro over the top and give one final toss. Taste for salt and add a pinch more if needed. The finished aloo gobi should taste of nothing but the vegetables themselves and the spices — deeply savory, warmly spiced, with a clean lemony lift. Serve immediately with gluten-free flatbread or gluten-free flatbread. It does not hold well; the vegetables lose their texture as they sit.
fr-amatriciana: Place the guanciale in a cold, dry, heavy skillet — a wide sauté pan or frying pan works well. Set over medium-low heat and cook slowly, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the fat renders out completely and the pieces are golden, amber, and slightly crisp but still yielding at the centre. The guanciale releases its fat slowly — starting in a cold pan allows the fat to liquefy gradually and coat the pieces evenly as they cook. Remove the guanciale with a slotted spoon, leaving all the rendered fat in the pan.

Add the chilli flakes to the guanciale fat in the pan over medium heat and stir for 30 seconds until the chilli blooms in the fat — it will sizzle gently and the fat will turn faintly orange-red. Immediately pour in the white wine and stir vigorously to dissolve any fond and combine the chilli into the liquid. Let the wine reduce by half over 2–3 minutes until the raw alcohol smell cooks off and is replaced by a mellow, slightly fruity fragrance.

Crush the San Marzano tomatoes through your fingers into the pan — keeping them in rough, irregular pieces rather than a smooth purée. Return the guanciale to the pan. Stir well to combine, then let the sauce simmer uncovered over medium heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the tomatoes have broken down, the sauce has thickened to a rich, rust-red slick, and the fat from the guanciale is beginning to float in orange droplets on the surface — a sign of proper concentration.

Cook the bucatini in heavily salted boiling water to just shy of al dente (1–2 minutes less than the package says). Reserve 120 ml of the starchy cooking water before draining. Transfer the pasta directly to the sauce in the pan using tongs, bringing some cooking water naturally. Add a splash of reserved water and toss vigorously over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until the pasta finishes cooking in the sauce and the sauce clings to every tube. Add more water as needed — the sauce should coat, not pool. Finish with a grinding of black pepper.

Divide the pasta into warmed bowls. Scatter a generous amount of finely grated Pecorino Romano over each portion — it should be enough to see as a visible, snowy layer over the sauce. The cheese will soften and partially melt into the hot pasta, providing a sharp, salty counterpoint to the rich, sweet-porky sauce. Serve immediately. No additional oil, cream, or butter. The dish is complete.

fr-anticuchos: Working on a sturdy board, examine the beef heart carefully. Using a sharp boning knife, trim away any visible pockets of exterior fat — they are tallow-flavored and won't render in the short grill time. More importantly, feel for and cut out the firm white connective tissue tubes (the aorta and pulmonary vessels) that run through the top of the heart, and peel away the tough outer membrane that sheathes the ventricle walls. The actual muscle of the heart is unlike any other cut — it is deep red, extremely fine-grained, and dense, with almost no intramuscular fat. Slice the cleaned muscle across the grain into pieces roughly 3cm thick. They should look like small, irregular medallions, darker and more uniform than a steak.

In the bowl with the trimmed heart pieces, combine the ají panca paste, red wine vinegar, minced garlic, ground cumin, salt, and black pepper. Mix thoroughly with your hands, massaging the marinade into every surface and crevice of the meat. The vinegar begins a gentle acid tenderization immediately, and the ají panca — which is smoky, mild, and fruity in a distinctly different way from ají amarillo — stains the meat a deep, brick-red purple. Cover the bowl tightly and refrigerate for a minimum of 3 hours, ideally overnight. The longer it marinates (up to 24 hours), the more the vinegar softens the tight muscle fibers and the more deeply the spices penetrate. An hour before cooking, thread the pieces onto metal skewers — two or three pieces per skewer, leaving a little space between them.

Prepare your grill for extremely high direct heat — charcoal is authentic and optimal, gas works but lacks the smoke. The grill grate should be so hot that the skewers sizzle immediately and loudly on contact. Brush the grate with a little oil to prevent sticking. Lay the skewers perpendicular to the grate bars and leave them absolutely still for 2–3 minutes to develop a deep char. Turn once; grill the second side for 2 more minutes. Total cooking time is 4–5 minutes — beef heart is best eaten medium, with a faint blush of pink in the very center of the thick pieces. If you cook it beyond that, the muscle fibers contract violently and the texture goes from pleasantly chewy-tender to genuinely tough. While grilling, baste once with oil to create additional flare-ups and the characteristic flame-kissed char marks of street-cooked anticuchos.

Let the skewers rest 2 minutes off the heat. Plate in the traditional Lima street-food style: the skewers laid directly over rounds of boiled choclo (or corn on the cob cut into rounds) and boiled potato — the mild starchiness of both counterbalances the charred, acidic, deeply savory heart. In Lima, an anticucho vendor will hand you the skewer with the corn and potato already impaled at the base, so each bite can alternate between meat and starch. No additional sauce is strictly necessary, but a spoonful of remaining marinade warmed and reduced makes an excellent quick dipping sauce, or serve with additional ají amarillo paste on the side.
fr-apple-pie: In a large bowl, whisk flour and salt. Add cold butter and lard. Using your fingertips, work the fats into the flour until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs with some larger, flat butter flakes — those flakes create the flaky layers. Do not overwork. Drizzle in ice water 1 tablespoon at a time, tossing with a fork. Stop adding water when the dough just holds together when pinched. Divide in two, flatten into discs, wrap, and refrigerate at least 2 hours or overnight.

Combine the sliced apples with sugar, cinnamon, cornstarch, and lemon juice. Toss to coat. Let stand 30 minutes at room temperature — the sugar will draw liquid out of the apples. Drain off the released juice into a small saucepan, reduce it to a thick syrup over medium heat, and pour it back over the apples. This pre-reducing step prevents the gap that forms between crust and filling when juices boil away during baking.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the first dough disc to a 30 cm circle, about 3–4 mm thick. Drape into a 23 cm pie dish, pressing into the corners without stretching. Pile the apple filling into the shell, mounding it higher than the rim — it will settle during baking. Roll the second disc and lay it over the top, or cut into strips for a lattice. Trim to 1.5 cm overhang, fold under, and crimp the edge. Cut steam vents if using a full top crust. Refrigerate the assembled pie for 30 minutes before baking.

Preheat oven to 220 C (425 F) with a sheet pan on the lower rack (this conducts heat to the bottom crust). Brush the top crust with egg wash and scatter a pinch of granulated sugar over it. Bake at 220 C for 20 minutes until the edges begin to set and color. Reduce heat to 190 C (375 F) and continue baking 35–45 minutes until the crust is deeply golden and the filling is visibly bubbling through the vents. Cool on a wire rack for at least 3 hours before slicing — the filling thickens as it cools.

fr-apple-strudel: Combine flour, warm water, oil, and salt, mixing until a shaggy dough forms. Knead vigorously for 10 full minutes — this dough requires serious development of gluten, which is what allows it to be stretched to an almost impossible thinness without tearing. Knead by slapping the dough against the work surface and folding it. The finished dough should be smooth as silk, warm from the kneading, and extremely elastic. Shape into a ball, brush with oil, and rest covered for 45 minutes at room temperature. The rest is not optional — it relaxes the gluten to the point where stretching becomes possible.

Toss the thinly sliced apples with sugar and cinnamon and let macerate for 15 minutes — the sugar draws out juice. Drain the excess juice thoroughly, as too much moisture will make the strudel soggy. Toast the breadcrumbs in butter until golden and fragrant — these absorb any residual apple moisture during baking, keeping the pastry crisp from inside. Combine the drained apples and buttered breadcrumbs just before filling the stretched dough.

Cover a large table with a clean cloth and dust lightly with flour. Place the rested dough in the center and roll it out with a pin to about 40x60cm. Then begin stretching by hand: place both hands under the dough, palms down, and stretch outward from the center using the backs of your knuckles. Walk around the table, stretching in all directions, until the dough is paper-thin (about 1mm) and almost transparent — roughly 60x80cm. The dough must be so thin you can read text through it. Brush thoroughly with melted butter as you work.

Spread the buttered breadcrumbs across two-thirds of the dough, leaving a 5cm border. Pile the apple filling evenly over the breadcrumbs. Using the tablecloth to assist, roll the strudel into a tight log, using the cloth to lift and fold rather than your hands. Place seam-side down on a parchment-lined baking sheet, curving into a horseshoe if needed. Brush generously with melted butter. Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 35–40 minutes, brushing with butter once more at the 20-minute mark. Dust with powdered sugar and serve warm.
fr-apple-tarte-tatin: Scatter the caster sugar in an even layer across the base of a heavy 24–26 cm oven-safe skillet or tarte tatin mold. Set over medium heat without stirring. The sugar will begin to liquefy at the edges — let it pool before swirling the pan gently to even the color. Continue until the liquid caramel reaches a deep amber, the color of dark mahogany. Remove from heat.

Off the heat, drop the cold butter pieces into the amber caramel one at a time. Add the vanilla seeds and pod. The mixture will bubble furiously — this is correct. Stir with a heatproof spatula until the butter is fully incorporated and the caramel is smooth, glossy, and homogeneous.

Remove the vanilla pod. Arrange the apple halves cut-side up over the caramel, packing them as tightly as possible in a circular pattern — they will shrink during cooking, so crowding is correct. Set the pan over medium heat and cook 15–20 minutes until the apples are partially softened and the caramel has deepened and thickened around them.

Cut the pastry into a circle 2 cm wider than the pan diameter. Drape it over the apples and tuck the overhanging edge down into the pan, hugging the apple perimeter. Prick the pastry six times with a fork. Preheat the oven to 190°C (375°F) fan-assisted.

Bake at 190°C for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is deeply golden and puffed, and caramel is visibly bubbling at the pan edges. Remove and rest on a wire rack for exactly 5 minutes — no longer, or the caramel will seize and the tart will stick on inversion.

Place a large, lipped serving plate firmly over the pan. Grip both plate and pan securely, count to one, then invert with confidence. Hold for three seconds, then lift the pan away. Any apples that have shifted can be pressed gently back into place with a spoon. Serve warm with crème fraîche alongside.

Cut the pastry into a circle 2 cm wider than the pan diameter. Drape it over the apples and tuck the overhanging edge down into the pan, hugging the apple perimeter. Prick the pastry six times with a fork. Preheat the oven to 190°C (375°F) fan-assisted.

Bake at 190°C for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is deeply golden and puffed, and caramel is visibly bubbling at the pan edges. Remove and rest on a wire rack for exactly 5 minutes — no longer, or the caramel will seize and the tart will stick on inversion.

Place a large, lipped serving plate firmly over the pan. Grip both plate and pan securely, count to one, then invert with confidence. Hold for three seconds, then lift the pan away. Any apples that have shifted can be pressed gently back into place with a spoon. Serve warm with crème fraîche alongside.
fr-arancini: Combine the rice and warm stock or water in a medium saucepan. Add the saffron water and a generous pinch of salt. Bring to a boil, stir once, then reduce to a low simmer and cover. Cook for 16-18 minutes until all liquid is absorbed. The rice should be slightly firmer than eating-rice — it will continue to absorb and compact as it cools. Immediately spread the rice onto a large rimmed baking sheet in a thin, even layer to cool. Do not cover — you want steam to escape. Let cool completely at room temperature, at least 45 minutes, until the rice is sticky, compact, and cold to the touch. Cold rice is non-negotiable for forming arancini.

Cook the diced onion in a little oil over medium heat until soft and translucent, about 8 minutes. Add the ground meat and cook, breaking it up with a wooden spoon, until no pink remains and the meat is lightly browned in spots, about 10 minutes. Add the tomato paste and stir to coat. Cook for 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until the paste darkens and smells sweet and caramelized. Add a splash of water or wine to deglaze. Season well with salt and pepper. Simmer on low heat for 20 minutes until the mixture is thick, cohesive, and not at all wet — a wet filling will burst the rice shell during frying. Cool completely before filling.

Transfer the cold, spread rice to a large bowl. Beat one egg and add it to the rice. Mix thoroughly with your hands until the egg is fully distributed and the rice feels even more cohesive and slightly sticky. This binding step makes the arancini hold their shape during breading and frying. Test by pressing a handful firmly — it should hold a firm ball that doesn't crumble.

Wet your hands lightly. Scoop about 100g of rice into one palm and flatten it into a disc roughly 10 cm across. Place a heaped teaspoon of cooled ragù in the center and press a cube of mozzarella alongside it. Carefully cup your hand and bring the edges of the rice disc up and around the filling, pressing firmly to enclose it completely. Use both hands to roll into a tight sphere. Press firmly — any air pocket or thin spot will cause the arancini to burst in the fryer. Repeat. Rest the formed balls on a parchment-lined tray as you go.

Set up a breading station: beaten egg in one bowl, fine breadcrumbs in another. Roll each arancino first in beaten egg until completely coated, letting the excess drip off. Then roll immediately in the breadcrumbs, pressing firmly on all sides to create a complete, even crust with no bare patches. Roll a second time through egg and breadcrumbs for a double coat — this double layer is the secret to a shatteringly crisp shell that won't crack in the oil. Place on a parchment-lined tray and refrigerate for at least 20 minutes before frying.

Heat the neutral oil in a deep, heavy pot to 175 C (350 F) — use a thermometer. The oil depth should be at least 8 cm to allow the arancini to be submerged. Gently lower 2-3 arancini into the oil at a time — do not crowd the pot, which drops the temperature and causes greasy, pale results. Fry for 4-5 minutes, turning gently with a spider skimmer every 90 seconds to ensure even color on all sides. Remove when deeply golden-brown all over and transfer to a wire rack lined with paper towels. Allow the oil to return to 175 C between batches. Serve within 5 minutes while the cheese is still molten.

fr-arroz-con-leche: Rinse the rice briefly under cold water. Combine milk, rice, cinnamon stick, lemon zest strips, and salt in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a gentle simmer, stirring frequently to prevent the milk from scorching on the base. Once it simmers, reduce to the lowest heat setting.

After 10 minutes, add the sugar and stir to dissolve. Continue cooking on the lowest heat, stirring every 3–4 minutes, for a total of 30–35 minutes from the point of adding the rice. The pudding is done when it has thickened to a loose, flowing cream — it should still look slightly underdone in the pot, as it will thicken further as it cools.

Remove the cinnamon stick and lemon zest strips. Stir in the butter until melted — it adds a silkiness that enriches the finish. Pour into individual serving bowls or one large dish. Press a piece of plastic wrap directly onto the surface of the pudding to prevent a skin from forming. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or until fully cold and set.

Remove the plastic wrap. Dust the surface with ground cinnamon through a fine sieve, tracing a neat stripe or covering the entire surface evenly. Serve immediately from the refrigerator — arroz con leche is best cold. Do not stir the cinnamon in; it sits on top as both flavour and visual mark of completion.
fr-arroz-rojo: Combine the tomatoes, garlic, and onion quarter in a blender with 100ml of the broth and blitz to a completely smooth purée. You should have approximately 350ml of liquid. The raw purée will be bright orange-red; it will deepen during cooking. Set aside.

Heat the oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the dry (unrinsed) rice all at once and stir constantly with a wooden spoon for 4–6 minutes. The grains will gradually turn from white to pale blond, then to a warm golden color. Do not walk away — toasting is what keeps Mexican rice grains separate rather than clumping. The room will fill with a nutty, popcorn-like aroma.

Add the carrot and serrano chile to the toasted rice and stir for 30 seconds. Pour in the tomato purée — it will hiss and spatter as it hits the hot oil — and stir immediately to coat all the grains. Add the remaining broth, cumin, and salt. Bring to a boil, stirring once, then reduce to the lowest possible heat, cover tightly, and cook undisturbed for 18–20 minutes.

Remove from heat. Scatter the frozen peas over the surface, re-cover, and let rest 5 minutes — the residual steam will thaw and warm the peas without cooking them to mush. Then use a fork to fluff gently from the edges inward, pulling the grains apart. Remove the serrano chile before serving if desired. Taste for salt.
fr-arroz-verde: Combine the poblano, jalapeño, cilantro (stems and all), onion, and garlic in a blender. Add 250 ml of the stock. Blitz on high for 60-90 seconds until completely smooth with no visible pieces. The purée will be a vivid, almost neon green at first — it will darken as it cooks. Season the purée lightly with salt before adding it to the rice. Measure it — you need approximately 500 ml of purée total; if you have more, reserve it. If less, add a little more stock.

Rinse the rice under cold water until the water runs clear, then spread it out on a clean kitchen towel and pat as dry as possible — wet rice will spatter violently in the hot oil and steam instead of toasting. Heat the oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid over medium-high heat until the oil shimmers. Add the dry rice and spread into an even layer. Cook, stirring constantly, for 4-5 minutes until the grains turn from white to a pale, even golden color and smell nutty and toasted.

Pour the entire green purée over the toasted rice all at once — it will hiss and spatter as it hits the hot oil and rice, so stand back. Stir immediately to prevent any rice from sticking. Cook over medium-high heat, stirring frequently, for 3-4 minutes as the purée dries out and the rice absorbs the green color. You are essentially frying the purée into the rice — when it no longer looks wet and the rice has absorbed the vivid green color, it is ready for the remaining stock.

Pour the remaining stock (250 ml) over the rice, add the salt, and stir once to distribute. Bring to a full boil over high heat. Once boiling, reduce to the absolute lowest heat, cover tightly, and cook for 15 minutes without lifting the lid. The rice needs to steam in this final stage — every time the lid is lifted, you lose steam and the rice will cook unevenly. Set a timer and do not open the pot.

Remove from heat and let the rice rest, covered, for 5 minutes to allow the steam to redistribute evenly through the grains. Uncover and fluff gently with a fork, using a lifting and separating motion from the bottom of the pot. Taste and adjust salt. The rice should be a deep, even green throughout each grain — not just surface-stained. Serve as a side dish alongside chicken, fish, or beans, or as a base for a grain bowl.
fr-baba-ghanoush: Place whole eggplants directly on a gas burner set to high flame, or as close as possible to a very hot grill or broiler element. Char on all sides, turning with tongs every 3–4 minutes, until the entire exterior is blackened and the eggplant has completely collapsed and feels hollow. This takes 15–20 minutes total. The more thoroughly charred, the deeper the smoke.

Place the charred eggplants in a colander over a bowl. Cover the colander and let them steam for 10 minutes — this loosens the skin and allows the eggplant to release bitter liquid. Peel away all the charred skin with your fingers, working carefully to remove any large patches of black. Discard the liquid that has collected. Allow the drained flesh to sit for a further 5 minutes to shed more liquid.

Using a fork or pestle, mash the garlic with the salt to a smooth paste. Add the eggplant flesh and mash roughly — some texture is welcome. Beat in the tahini and lemon juice in alternating additions, tasting as you go. The dip will tighten and turn creamy as the tahini emulsifies with the eggplant. Adjust salt and lemon aggressively — it needs more than you expect. Transfer to a serving plate, make a well with the back of a spoon, drizzle with olive oil, dust with paprika, and scatter parsley.
fr-baja-fish-tacos: Combine the flour-cornstarch blend, cayenne, garlic powder, and salt in a medium bowl. Pour in the cold beer all at once and stir with a fork just until combined — 8 to 10 strokes at most. The batter must be lumpy, not smooth. Lumps of unmixed flour are your friend: they create uneven pockets that fry into extra-crunchy patches. Do not over-mix. Keep the batter cold — set the bowl over ice if your kitchen is warm. Cold batter hits hot oil and creates maximum shatter.

Heat at least 5 cm of oil in a heavy pot or deep skillet to 180°C (350°F). Use a thermometer — temperature precision matters here. Cut the fish into 2 x 8 cm strips along the grain. Pat them bone-dry with paper towels, then season with salt. Working in batches of 3–4 strips (never crowd the pot), dip each strip into the batter, let the excess drip off for 3 seconds, then lower it into the oil away from you. Fry for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until the batter is a deep golden amber and the fish floats freely in the oil. Drain on a wire rack — not paper towels, which steam the crust soft.

Set a dry cast-iron skillet or comal over high heat. Toast each corn tortilla directly on the hot surface for 20–30 seconds per side until it puffs slightly, smells of toasted masa, and develops faint char spots. Stack and wrap in a clean cloth to keep warm and pliable — cold, stiff tortillas crack when folded around the fish.

Working quickly while the fish is still hot and crisp, lay two warmed tortillas slightly overlapping on a plate (Baja style uses two per taco for structural support). Add a strip of fried fish down the centre. Top with a loose mound of shredded cabbage, a generous drizzle of crema, a squeeze of lime, and a dash of hot sauce. Eat immediately — batter crust softens within 5 minutes of contact with moist toppings.

fr-baked-feta-greens-and-beans: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). In a 23 x 33 cm baking dish, toss the beans, cherry tomatoes, garlic, 45 ml of the olive oil, oregano, pepper flakes, and stock. Season with a small pinch of salt (the feta will add plenty) and lots of black pepper. Spread in an even layer.
Bake uncovered for 15 minutes, until the tomatoes begin to split and the liquid is bubbling at the edges.

Nestle the feta block in the center. Toss the kale with the remaining 15 ml oil and a pinch of salt and pile it around the feta. Bake 15–20 minutes more until the kale is wilted with crisp tips and the feta is soft. Then switch to broil (high) for 2–3 minutes, watching closely, to brown the top of the cheese.

Grate the lemon zest over the top and squeeze over half the juice. Gently break up the feta with a spoon, swirling it into the beans and greens so it thickens the juices into a creamy sauce. Taste, add more lemon if needed, and serve with torn gluten-free bread.
fr-banana-oat-snack-cake: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease an 8 × 8 in (20 × 20 cm) square pan and line it with a parchment sling. In a large bowl, mash the bananas with a fork until mostly smooth. Whisk in the brown sugar, eggs, melted butter, yogurt, and vanilla until evenly combined.

Add the flour, oats, baking soda, salt, and cinnamon directly to the bowl (sprinkle the baking soda evenly so it doesn't clump) and fold with a spatula just until no dry flour remains. Rest the batter 5 minutes so the oats begin to soften, then scrape into the pan, smooth the top, and scatter with the pumpkin seeds.

Bake on the middle rack 30–38 minutes, until the top is golden brown and domed, the edges pull from the pan, and a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean or with a few moist crumbs. Cool in the pan on a rack at least 20 minutes, then lift out with the parchment and cut into 9 or 16 squares.

fr-banh-mi-pork: Combine sliced pork with fish sauce, shallots, lemongrass, and black pepper. Toss to coat every surface thoroughly. Marinate at room temperature for 30 minutes, or refrigerate up to 4 hours. The fish sauce begins drawing moisture out of the meat, concentrating the brine.

In a wide heavy skillet or wok over medium heat, add oil then sugar in an even layer. Do not stir — let it melt and color. When the edges turn amber, gently swirl the pan. Pull from heat at a deep amber that smells like butterscotch, not burnt coffee. Work fast; caramel moves through its stages in seconds.

Add marinated pork to the caramel in a single layer, working quickly. The mixture will spit and bubble violently — step back. Do not stir for the first 90 seconds so a crust can form. Then toss and cook over medium-high for 4-5 minutes total, until edges char and sauce clings like lacquer.

Remove from heat. Add 2 tablespoons of water to deglaze any stuck caramel from the pan and toss the pork to coat in the loose sauce. Let rest in the pan for 2 minutes — the residual heat melds the glaze and the resting reduces the risk of burning your mouth on the caramelized edges.
fr-banh-xeo-batter: In a large mixing bowl, combine the rice flour, cornstarch, turmeric, and salt. Whisk together the dry ingredients first so the turmeric is evenly distributed — it tends to clump and will cause yellow streaks in the finished crepe if not fully dispersed in the rice flour before liquid is added. Pour in the coconut milk while whisking, then add the cold water in a steady stream, continuing to whisk until completely smooth and lump-free. The batter should be very thin — thinner than pancake batter, closer to the consistency of heavy cream. The turmeric will dye the batter a vivid golden-yellow. Rest the batter for at least 30 minutes to allow the rice flour to fully hydrate and the starches to relax.

After the 30-minute rest, stir the sliced spring onions into the batter. The rested batter will have settled slightly with a thin waterier layer on top — stir it back together before stirring in the scallions. The spring onions are added to the batter rather than the filling so that they get lightly crisped by the pan heat during cooking, adding a gentle allium sweetness and a faint char to the crepe itself. Stir just before pouring each crepe, as the scallions and starch will continue to settle.

Heat a 28 cm non-stick frying pan over high heat until smoking hot — this is not negotiable. Add the oil and swirl to coat. Pour in one ladleful (about 80–100 ml) of batter, immediately lifting the pan and tilting in a circular motion so the batter spreads thinly across the entire surface, almost like making a crepe. The batter should sizzle explosively the instant it hits the pan — the Vietnamese name bánh xèo literally refers to that sizzling sound. Reduce heat to medium and add the filling (shrimp, pork, bean sprouts) to one half of the crepe. Cover with a lid and cook for 2–3 minutes until the edges of the crepe are golden and lifting away from the pan spontaneously, then uncover and cook for 1 more minute to crisp the edges fully. Fold the unfilled half over the filled half and slide onto a plate.

Serve each bánh xèo immediately as it comes from the pan. In the traditional Southern Vietnamese style, the diner tears off pieces of the crisp crepe, wraps each piece in a large lettuce leaf with fresh herbs (mint, perilla, Vietnamese coriander) and rolls the whole thing into a bundle to dip into nước chấm. The contrast between the crisp, hot crepe and the cool, fresh herbs wrapped around it is the defining pleasure of the dish. The crepe will soften within 2 minutes of folding — bánh xèo cannot be held; it must be eaten the moment it is made.
fr-basque-burnt-cheesecake: Beat cream cheese with sugar and salt in a stand mixer with the paddle attachment on medium speed — or with a hand mixer — until the mixture is completely smooth, fluffy, and light, about 3 minutes. Scrape down the bowl twice. No lumps are acceptable here — cold cream cheese leaves clumps that never fully dissolve in the oven.

Add eggs one at a time on low speed, mixing until just incorporated before adding the next. Add vanilla with the final egg. Do not rush this step — adding eggs too quickly causes the emulsion to break. Scrape the bowl after each addition.

Sift flour directly into the batter. Add heavy cream. Whisk gently by hand until everything is incorporated — do not use the electric mixer at this stage. The batter should be thin, pourable, and completely smooth. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a jug for easy pouring.

Preheat oven to 230 C (450 F) conventional, or 210 C (410 F) fan. Line a 20 cm (8 inch) springform pan with two sheets of parchment, pushing them up the sides — the paper will ruffle and buckle and that is perfectly traditional. Pour in the batter. Bake for 28–32 minutes, until the top is deeply scorched — nearly burnt — with a dark mahogany center and the entire interior wobbles dramatically when the pan is nudged.

Cool the cheesecake in the pan at room temperature for at least 1 hour — it will deflate dramatically as it cools, developing the characteristic sunken center. Refrigerate for a minimum of 3 hours (overnight is ideal) to allow the custard to fully set. Serve at room temperature for the most custardy texture: remove from fridge 30 minutes before slicing.

fr-bbq-pulled-pork: Combine brown sugar, smoked paprika, salt, and spice mix in a bowl. Pat the pork shoulder completely dry with paper towels. Apply the rub all over the shoulder — every surface, including the crevices around the bone. Press firmly so the rub adheres. Wrap tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. The salt will draw moisture to the surface and then reabsorb it, seasoning deep into the meat.

Set up your smoker or oven at 107–121°C. For smokers, use hickory, apple, or cherry wood. Place pork fat-cap up. Smoke for 5–6 hours, maintaining temperature, until an instant-read thermometer reads 74°C internally. Spritz with apple cider vinegar every 90 minutes to keep the bark moist and add tang. The bark will form and harden during this phase — do not wrap yet.

When the internal temperature stalls between 65–74°C (the infamous BBQ 'stall' caused by evaporative cooling), tightly wrap the pork in two layers of butcher paper or heavy foil. Add a splash of apple cider vinegar inside the wrap. Return to the smoker or move to a 135°C oven. Cook until the internal temperature reaches 93–96°C, approximately 2–3 more hours.

Remove the wrapped pork from heat when it reaches 93–96°C. Without unwrapping, wrap the entire package in a towel and place in a cooler for at least 1 hour, up to 4 hours. This rest is not optional — it allows the temperature to equalize throughout the shoulder and lets the gelatin re-set, which means juicier, more cohesive pulled pork.

Unwrap the pork over a large pan to catch all the juices. Using two forks or heat-resistant gloves, pull the meat apart into shaggy strands. Discard any large pieces of pure fat. Pour some of the collected pan juices back over the pulled pork to keep it moist. Serve with BBQ sauce on the side — never mix it in, so diners can control their sauce level.
fr-beef-and-barley-stew: Pat the beef very dry and season with 10 g of the salt and the pepper. Heat 30 ml oil in a heavy 6–7 litre Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Brown the beef in 3 batches, leaving space between cubes, 3–4 minutes per side for 2 sides, until deeply crusted. Transfer to a bowl. Don't clean the pot.

Reduce heat to medium and add the remaining 15 ml oil, onions, celery, and mushrooms. Cook 8–10 minutes, scraping up fond as the vegetables release moisture, until the mushrooms are browned and the liquid has evaporated. Add garlic and tomato paste and cook 2 minutes, stirring, until the paste darkens to brick red.

Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C). Pour in the stock and Worcestershire, scraping the pot clean. Return the beef and its juices, add thyme and bay, and bring to a simmer on the stovetop. Cover and braise in the oven 1 hour 30 minutes. (Stovetop alternative: the lowest simmer with the lid slightly ajar, stirring every 20 minutes.)

Stir in the barley, carrots, and the remaining 5 g salt, making sure the barley is submerged (add 250 ml water if the liquid sits below the solids). Cover and return to the oven for 45–50 minutes, stirring once, until the barley is plump and tender and the beef is fork-tender.

Remove the thyme stems and bay leaves. Skim excess fat from the surface. Taste and adjust salt and pepper; scatter with parsley. To freeze: cool uncovered in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours; freeze up to 3 months. The barley keeps absorbing liquid in storage, so add 150–250 ml water or stock per quart when reheating to a steady simmer.

fr-beef-bourguignon: In a heavy Dutch oven over medium heat, cook the lardons in a dry pot until the fat renders and the dice turn golden and crisp, 6-8 minutes. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and reserve, leaving the rendered fat behind to sear the beef. Do not let the fat smoke and scorch.

Raise the heat to medium-high. Season the bone-dry beef cubes generously with salt and pepper. Sear them in small batches in the hot fat, leaving space between pieces, until each face is a deep brown crust — about 2 minutes a side. Crowding steams the meat grey; patience builds the fond. Remove the beef and set it aside with the lardons.

Lower the heat to medium. Add the mirepoix to the pot and cook in the beef fat until softened and lightly caramelised, 8-10 minutes, scraping the fond loose as the vegetables release moisture. Stir in the garlic and tomato paste and cook until the paste darkens from bright red to brick and smells toasty, about 2 minutes.

Sprinkle the flour over the vegetables and stir for 1-2 minutes to cook out the raw taste. Pour in the entire bottle of red wine, scraping the pot floor to dissolve all the fond. Bring to a brisk simmer and let it reduce by about a third, 8-10 minutes — this burns off the harsh alcohol and concentrates the wine into a true sauce base.

Return the beef and lardons to the pot along with any juices. Pour in enough warm stock to almost cover the meat and tuck in the bouquet garni. Bring to a bare simmer, then cover and transfer to a 150°C / 300°F oven (or hold the gentlest stovetop simmer). Cook for 2.5-3 hours until the beef is fork-tender, turning the meat once halfway through.

While the beef rests, sauté the pearl onions and mushrooms in a little butter until golden and glazed. If the braising sauce is thin, simmer it uncovered to reduce, skimming any fat from the surface. Fold the beef, lardons, onions and mushrooms back into the sauce, warm through gently, and correct the seasoning. Rest 10 minutes off the heat before serving.

fr-beef-bulgogi: Place the beef in the freezer for 30–45 minutes until firm but not frozen solid — a light crust of frost on the exterior, yielding interior. Using a very sharp knife, slice against the grain as thin as you can manage: 2–3 mm is ideal. Partially frozen meat holds its structure under the blade, allowing cuts that would be impossible with room-temperature beef. Fan the slices in a wide, shallow dish for marinating.

Whisk soy sauce, grated pear, sesame oil, sugar, garlic, ginger, scallion whites, and pepper until the sugar fully dissolves. Pour over the fanned beef slices. With clean hands, massage the marinade into each slice, separating them to ensure full coverage. Cover and refrigerate. Marinate a minimum of 2 hours; 4 hours is the sweet spot. Beyond 8 hours, pear enzymes begin to compromise the beef texture.

Heat a cast iron pan or grill to the highest possible heat until smoking. Work in very small batches — a single layer of slices covering no more than a third of the pan surface. The sugar in the marinade caramelizes instantly on a screaming-hot surface; crowding drops the pan temperature and produces steaming instead of searing. Cook each batch 60–90 seconds per side. The caramelization happens in the first 30 seconds of contact.

Pile the seared bulgogi on a serving platter. Scatter toasted sesame seeds and the reserved scallion greens over the top. Serve immediately alongside steamed short-grain rice, kimchi, and banchan. For ssam, provide perilla leaves and rice for wrapping.

fr-beef-goulash: Melt the lard in a heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the diced onions with a pinch of salt. Cook slowly, stirring often, for 15–20 minutes until the onions are deeply golden and jammy. Do not rush this step — the sweetness of the onion is the backbone of the entire dish.

Remove the pot from heat completely — this is critical. Stir in the paprika and garlic off the flame. The residual heat will cook the spice enough to open its fat-soluble color compounds without burning it. Paprika burns at a very low temperature and turns bitter in seconds over direct heat. Stir for 30–45 seconds until the mixture is a vivid, uniform red paste.

Return the pot to medium-high heat. Add the beef cubes and season with salt and caraway seeds. Stir to coat every piece with the paprika base. Allow the beef to color on at least two sides — about 3–4 minutes per side without moving. Work in batches if needed to avoid steaming. The goal is a fond-building sear, not full browning.

Add enough stock to barely cover the beef. Scrape up any fond from the bottom. Bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest simmer — just a bubble breaking the surface every few seconds. Cover and cook for 1 hour 30 minutes. Check occasionally and add a splash of water if the liquid drops below one-third the height of the meat. The stew is done when the beef yields completely to a fork with no resistance.
fr-beef-rendang: Combine the shallots, garlic, ginger, chilies, candlenuts, ground coriander, and turmeric in a blender or food processor. Add a small splash of water to get it moving and blend to a completely smooth paste with no visible chunks — this is the rempah, the fragrant paste that is the soul of Indonesian cooking. Alternatively, pound in a pestle and mortar for a coarser, more textured paste with greater aromatic complexity. The goal is a homogeneous mass where all aromatics are fully broken down. This step releases the volatile oils in the aromatics that will perfume the entire dish.

Heat a large, wide, heavy-bottomed pot or wok over medium heat — no added oil is needed yet as the coconut milk fat will provide it. Add the rempah paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 8–12 minutes until the paste has darkened from bright orange to a deep, toasted red-brown and the raw, sharp smell has transformed into something roasted and complex. The paste will stick and resist the spoon — keep stirring and scraping from the bottom. Add the galangal, bruised lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves, and turmeric leaf. Fry together for 2 minutes more until the aromatic leaves release their oils into the paste.

Add the beef chunks to the fried rempah and stir to coat every piece in the paste. Pour in all the coconut milk, then add the kerisik, palm sugar, and salt. Stir to combine. Bring to a vigorous boil, then reduce to a steady, visible simmer. Cook uncovered, stirring every 15–20 minutes, for 2.5–3 hours. The coconut milk will go through distinct phases: first a pale, bubbling liquid; then a thickening, yellowing sauce as the fat separates; then a progressively darkening gravy as moisture evaporates and the sugars concentrate. The beef chunks will soften completely and then firm up again slightly in the final dry-frying phase.

Once the liquid is nearly gone and the separated coconut oil is visibly frying the meat and paste, lower the heat to the minimum and stir constantly with a wooden spoon or spatula. The rendang will darken rapidly at this stage as the sugars caramelize and the spice crust on the beef deepens from dark brown to near-black. Fry in this dry state for 10–20 minutes, turning the beef frequently, until the pieces are uniformly dark and the paste coating has dried to a matte finish. The beef should be tender but slightly chewy — not fall-apart soft, not dry. Remove and discard the lemongrass, galangal, and lime leaves before serving.

fr-beef-tartare: Keep the beef in the freezer for 15–20 minutes before cutting — a partially firm fillet is dramatically easier to cut cleanly. This is not to freeze it but to firm the fibers so the knife glides rather than drags. The beef must remain red, not grey; it should be cold to the touch at the core but not frozen solid. All bowls, the cutting board, and the knife should be chilled as well if working in a warm kitchen.

Using a sharp, heavy chef's knife, first slice the beef across the grain into 4 mm planks. Stack the planks and cut into 4 mm batons. Rotate and cut into 4 mm dice. Gather the dice and run the knife through them once or twice to break up any larger pieces — you want 3–4 mm irregular cubes, not a paste. Do not use a food processor; it purees rather than cuts, yielding a rubbery, homogeneous texture. The goal is pieces small enough to meld with the dressing but large enough to retain the clean, iron-rich flavor of the beef.

In a cold bowl, combine the Dijon, Worcestershire, cognac (if using), and egg yolk, whisking briefly to blend. Add the shallot, capers, and parsley. Fold in the hand-cut beef using a fork — do not use your hands, which will warm the meat. Season aggressively with salt and pepper, tasting as you go. Raw beef needs noticeably more salt than you expect; under-seasoned tartare tastes flat and bloody. The mustard and capers carry acidity; the Worcestershire and egg yolk provide binding and depth. Taste. Adjust. Taste again. The mix should taste bright, savory, and boldly seasoned — not timid.

Press the tartare into a ring mold set on a chilled plate, or form a neat mound by hand using two spoons. If presenting formally, create a shallow well on top and nestle an extra egg yolk in the shell. Arrange cornichons, extra capers, and toasted bread around the plate. Serve within 5 minutes of plating — the acid and salt will continue to break down the beef. Raw beef served cold on a cold plate.

Heat the oil in a heavy pan until shimmering and just smoking, then sear the fillet on every face — including the ends — for about 60-90 seconds each, until a deep brown crust forms. The goal is colour and flavour, not cooking the inside. Lift it out and let it rest and cool completely; searing a warm fillet then wrapping it would steam the pastry.

Blitz or finely chop the mushrooms to a coarse paste. Cook them with the shallots, garlic and thyme in a dry or barely-oiled pan over medium-high heat, stirring often. The mushrooms will release a flood of water — keep cooking, 15-20 minutes, until every drop has evaporated and the mass darkens into a thick, dry, intensely savoury duxelles. Season and cool completely. Any residual moisture here will turn the pastry to paste.

Lay overlapping sheets of prosciutto on a large sheet of cling film to form a rectangle big enough to enclose the fillet. Spread the cooled duxelles evenly over the ham. Brush the cooled fillet all over with mustard, lay it along the edge of the duxelles, and use the cling film to roll the ham and mushroom tightly around the beef into a firm, even log. Twist the ends like a cracker to compress it, then chill for at least 20 minutes to set the shape.

Roll the chilled puff pastry into a rectangle large enough to enclose the log with a little overlap. Unwrap the chilled log onto the pastry, brush the pastry edges with egg yolk, and roll it up, sealing the seam underneath and pressing out any air. Trim and tuck the ends, sealing them with egg wash. Chill the parcel 15-20 minutes so the pastry stays cold, then brush all over with egg yolk, score the top lightly in a diagonal lattice, and sprinkle with flaky salt.

Bake on a preheated tray in a hot oven (200°C / 400°F) for 35-45 minutes, until the pastry is deep golden and crisp all over. Use a meat thermometer pushed into the centre of the beef: pull it at 50-52°C / 122-126°F for a rosy medium-rare, as it will carry over while resting. Rest the Wellington on a board for a full 10-15 minutes before slicing — this lets the juices settle so they don't flood out and sog the crust. Carve into thick slices with a serrated knife.
fr-beer-batter-fish: Sift the flour, cornstarch, baking powder, salt, and cayenne together into a large, wide bowl. Make a well in the center. Your beer must be ice cold — if it's been at room temperature, rest the bottle in an ice bath for at least 20 minutes, or pop it in the freezer for 10. Cold beer retains more carbon dioxide, which is the structural backbone of the batter's crispness. Pour the cold beer into the well all at once and whisk with a balloon whisk, working quickly from the center outward. Mix only until just combined — the batter should still have a few small lumps. Overmixing develops gluten, which makes the crust chewy rather than crisp. The finished batter should have the consistency of thin double cream, coating a spoon but dripping off in a slow stream. If it's too thick, add a splash more cold beer; if too thin, sift in a tablespoon more flour. Place the bowl in the refrigerator or over ice while you heat the oil.

Pour the oil into a large, deep pot or Dutch oven to a depth of at least 8 cm (3 inches). Heat to exactly 190°C (375°F) — use a deep-fry thermometer. While the oil heats, pat the fish fillets completely dry with paper towels; surface moisture is the enemy of crisp batter. Season the fish lightly with salt on both sides. Set up a dredging station: a plate of plain flour, then the batter bowl. Working one fillet at a time, dredge the fish in plain flour, shaking off all excess — a whisper-thin flour coat helps the batter adhere and creates a steam barrier. Immediately lower the floured fillet into the batter, letting the excess drip back into the bowl for a count of three. Slowly lower the battered fillet into the hot oil, releasing it away from you. Do not overcrowd — fry one or two fillets at a time, or the oil temperature will drop and the batter will absorb fat instead of crisping. Fry for 6–8 minutes, turning once at the 3-minute mark, until the crust is deeply golden and audibly crackling. Drain on a wire rack over a baking sheet — not on paper towels, which trap steam underneath and soften the crust.

fr-beer-braised-chicken-onions: Pat thighs dry and season with 10 g salt and the pepper. Heat oil in a wide 5–6 litre Dutch oven over medium heat. Cook thighs skin-side down, in batches, 8–10 minutes until the skin is deeply golden and much of the fat has rendered; flip for 1 minute and set aside. Pour off all but about 2 tbsp fat.

Add butter, onions, and 2 g salt to the pot. Cook over medium to medium-low heat 25–30 minutes, stirring every few minutes and scraping the bottom, until the onions are soft, jammy, and a deep golden brown. If they start to stick or darken too quickly, add a splash of water and scrape.

Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C). Stir carrots and garlic into the onions for 2 minutes, then sprinkle over the flour and stir 1 minute. Pour in the beer and stock, scraping the bottom, and bring to a simmer. Add thyme and bay, nestle the chicken skin-side up with the skin above the liquid, and braise uncovered in the oven 45–50 minutes, until the thighs read at least 165°F (74°C) — ideally 185–195°F (85–90°C) — and the carrots are tender.

Remove the thyme stems and bay leaves. Stir the mustard and vinegar into the sauce around the chicken and taste for salt. Scatter with parsley. Serve with boiled potatoes, egg noodles, or thick-cut fries. To freeze: cool with the chicken covered in sauce, refrigerate within 2 hours, and freeze up to 3 months. Reheat covered at 350°F (175°C) until the chicken reaches 165°F (74°C).

fr-beet-borscht: In a bowl, toss the coarsely grated raw beets with all the apple cider vinegar and a pinch of salt. Toss thoroughly and set aside. This acidulation step is not optional: the acid reacts with the betalain pigments in the beet and stabilizes them, preventing the borscht from turning a dull brownish-purple during the long simmer. Acidulated beets maintain their vivid crimson color through cooking. The beets will immediately begin to weep their juice into the vinegar.

Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the diced onion and grated carrot and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft and translucent and the carrot has begun to soften, about 6–8 minutes. Push the vegetables to the sides and add the tomato paste to the center of the pot, pressing it against the hot metal. Cook the paste for 1–2 minutes, stirring, until it darkens slightly from bright red to deep brick — this pinçage deepens the tomato flavor and removes the tinned taste. Then stir the paste into the vegetables.

Add the acidulated beets and their liquid to the pot and stir well. Pour in all the stock. Add the bay leaves. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady, low simmer. The borscht should simmer, never boil hard, to develop flavor without making it murky. Cook for 15 minutes to begin building the base. The broth at this stage will be a vivid, deep crimson — this is the color you are working to preserve through the rest of the cook.

Add the shredded cabbage and diced potatoes to the simmering borscht. Stir to submerge and return to a simmer. Cook for 20–25 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender and beginning to thicken the broth slightly with their released starch, and the cabbage has fully softened and surrendered any raw crunch. The soup should remain at a gentle simmer throughout — a hard boil will make the potatoes break down too quickly and make the broth starchy and cloudy.

Add the crushed tomatoes, sugar, salt, and black pepper to the simmering pot. Stir well and taste carefully. Borscht is defined by the balance between sweet and sour: add vinegar a teaspoon at a time if it needs more brightness; add sugar or a grated beet if it needs more sweetness. The salt should be assertive — borscht can absorb considerable salt without tasting salty because of the acidity. Simmer for a final 5 minutes to marry the flavors, taste a final time, and remove the bay leaves.

Ladle the hot borscht into deep, warmed bowls. Place a generous dollop of cold sour cream directly in the center — the contrast of cold dairy against hot soup is part of the experience. Scatter freshly chopped dill generously over the top. The dill fragrance rising from the hot soup is one of the most distinctive smells in Eastern European cuisine. Serve with gluten-free bread or pampushky (Ukrainian garlic rolls) on the side.
fr-beignets: Combine all ingredients in a stand mixer bowl. Mix on low with a dough hook for 2 minutes to combine, then increase to medium and knead for 6-8 minutes. The dough will be soft, slightly tacky, and smooth — softer than pizza dough and just firm enough to hold its shape without spreading. Do not add extra flour; the softness is what creates the airy, hollow puff in the fryer.

Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with cling film, and proof at room temperature (25-28 C) for 1-1.5 hours, until doubled in size. Alternatively, refrigerate overnight for a slower, more flavourful proof — the cold also makes the dough easier to roll and cut cleanly. If refrigerating, remove 30 minutes before frying to take the chill off.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the proofed dough to 6 mm thickness — slightly thicker than you might expect. Cut into 6 x 6 cm squares using a sharp knife or pastry cutter. The edges should be clean cuts, not dragged. Lay the cut squares on a lightly floured tray and cover loosely with cling film. Allow to rest 15 minutes before frying — this second rest prevents toughness and encourages the initial puff.

Heat oil to 175 C (350 F) in a wide, heavy pot — minimum 8 cm depth. Fry 3-4 beignets at a time; do not crowd. Slide them in gently. Within 30 seconds they should begin to puff and float. Fry 90 seconds per side, flipping once. The beignet should puff dramatically hollow, like a small pillow inflated from within. Total fry time: 3 minutes. Drain on a rack, not paper.

Transfer hot beignets to a plate lined with a rack. Using a fine-mesh sieve, shower an extravagant quantity of icing sugar over each beignet from a height of 20 cm for maximum coverage and drift. The sugar must land on the hot surface — it will adhere and partially dissolve, creating the signature opaque white crust. Serve within 5 minutes, while the exterior is still crisp. Traditionally served three per order, with café au lait.
fr-berbere-lamb-shoulder: Pat the lamb pieces completely dry with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of a good sear. In a small bowl, mix 2 tablespoons of the berbere with the salt and rub this mixture thoroughly over every surface of the lamb. Work it into any natural seams and pockets. Allow to sit at room temperature for 30 minutes before searing — a cold piece of meat chills the pan and prevents proper Maillard browning.

Heat the niter kibbeh in a large heavy pot (Dutch oven) over high heat until it shimmers and begins to smoke lightly. Working in batches — never crowding the pot — sear the lamb pieces for 3-4 minutes per side until deeply browned, almost mahogany. The berbere spices will darken and bloom in the spiced butter, releasing an intoxicating, complex aroma. Press each piece firmly against the pot bottom with a spatula. Between batches, do not scrape up the fond — it will dissolve into the braise later.

In the same pot over medium heat, add the diced onion and cook in the remaining niter kibbeh and fond for 20-25 minutes until deeply golden — almost caramelized. This long, slow onion cook is fundamental to Ethiopian wat cooking. Add garlic and ginger, cook 2 minutes. Add the remaining berbere and stir for 1 minute to fry in the fat. Pour in the tej and scrape every bit of fond from the pot bottom — this is pure flavor. Add tomatoes and stock, stir to combine, then nestle the seared lamb pieces back in. The liquid should reach halfway up the meat. Bring to a simmer, cover tightly, and braise at 150°C in the oven or on the lowest stovetop flame for 3-4 hours.

Remove the lamb pieces to a warm plate. Increase heat under the braising liquid and boil uncovered for 10-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce reduces to a thick, glossy consistency that coats a spoon heavily. Skim any excess fat from the surface if desired — but some fat is traditional and carries the berbere's flavor. Return the lamb to the pot and baste with the reduced sauce. Taste and adjust salt. Serve over gluten-free flatbread (Ethiopian gluten-free flatbread) or rice, with additional sauce spooned over generously.
fr-bibimbap: Prepare each vegetable separately as namul. For spinach: blanch 30 seconds, shock in ice water, squeeze out every drop of water, then toss with a pinch of salt, half a teaspoon of sesame oil, and a small amount of minced garlic. For carrots: stir-fry in a dry pan 2 minutes until barely tender, season with salt and sesame oil. For bean sprouts: blanch 2 minutes, drain, toss with sesame oil and salt. For mushrooms: sauté in a drop of oil over medium-high until browned and any moisture has evaporated. Each vegetable should taste pleasantly seasoned on its own.

Mix the gochujang, sugar, sesame oil, and soy sauce in a small bowl until smooth and glossy. The sauce should taste hot, sweet, and savory in equal measure. Thin with one teaspoon of water if too thick to stir. This sauce is stirred into the bowl at the table — its richness and heat are the final seasoning of the dish.

Coat the inside of a stone dolsot bowl (or heavy cast-iron skillet) generously with the sesame oil and butter mixture. Place over medium-high heat on the stovetop and heat until the fat smokes. Add the cooked rice in an even layer, pressing it against the bottom and up the sides slightly. Reduce to medium and cook undisturbed for 5 to 7 minutes until you hear a steady, intense crackle from the base.

Working quickly while the bowl is screaming hot, arrange the seasoned namul in distinct piles around the perimeter of the rice — spinach, carrot, sprouts, and mushrooms in separate wedges, never mixed. Place a raw egg yolk or fried sunny-side-up egg in the center. Add a generous spoonful of bibimbap sauce beside the egg. Bring immediately to the table — the bowl continues crisping the rice through the meal. Each diner stirs everything together just before eating.
